title: Alpha CRM vs Beta CRM: which one should you pick
seoTitle: Alpha CRM vs Beta CRM (2026 Comparison)
description: A direct comparison of Alpha CRM and Beta CRM on price, trial length, and plan limits.
dek: Two CRMs aimed at the same small-team buyer, compared line by line.
Pricing, trial length, and plan ceilings, pulled straight from each vendor's own page.

blocks.html: Alpha CRM and Beta CRM compete for the same buyer: a small sales team that wants a pipeline without a long sales cycle to get started. The two tools land close together on price but differ in how they structure trials, free limits, and automation.
If you only read one section, read the pricing table below. Everything after it is the reasoning behind each row, in case a number alone does not tell you enough about which plan fits your team.

Alpha CRM starts at {{fact:alpha.price}}. Beta CRM's Team plan starts at {{fact:beta.price}}, and Beta CRM also sells a separate automation add-on at {{fact:beta.addon_price}} for teams that want sequences and workflow rules.

Stack the Beta CRM base plan and the automation add-on together and a team pays roughly {{calc:beta_bundle_price}} per seat per month, which puts it above Alpha CRM's single all-in price once automation is actually turned on.

Alpha CRM does not split automation into a separate line item, so its listed price already reflects what a team would pay to use the product fully, without an upsell waiting once the pipeline gets busier.

Alpha CRM offers a {{fact:alpha.trial}}, while Beta CRM's trial is shorter at {{fact:beta.trial}}. A longer trial matters more for a team that wants to load real pipeline data before deciding, rather than testing with a handful of sample deals.

On the free tier, Alpha CRM's limit is that {{fact:alpha.free_cap}}, while Beta CRM is tighter, since {{fact:beta.free_cap}}. Neither free tier is meant for a real team long-term, but Alpha CRM's version survives a slightly longer evaluation.

Once a team upgrades to a paid plan, Alpha CRM allows {{fact:alpha.contacts}}, well above Beta CRM's paid ceiling of {{fact:beta.contacts}}. A team with a larger contact list should weigh that gap carefully before picking Beta CRM on price alone.

Alpha CRM lists {{fact:alpha.integrations}}, compared with Beta CRM's {{fact:beta.integrations}}. Neither catalog is exhaustive, but Alpha CRM's is noticeably larger, which matters if your stack already includes a long tail of smaller tools.

Support is where the two diverge most: Alpha CRM offers {{fact:alpha.support}}, giving teams on a lower-cost plan a path to a human if something breaks. Beta CRM does not publish an equivalent phone-support tier at all on its pricing page.

Neither vendor charges extra fees to get started, and both publish every number used in this comparison on their own public pricing pages, so none of the figures above required a sales call to confirm.

faq.q: Which CRM is cheaper for a small team?
faq.a: Alpha CRM is cheaper once Beta CRM's automation add-on is included, though Beta CRM's base plan alone is close in price.

faq.q: Which has the longer free trial?
faq.a: Alpha CRM's trial runs longer than Beta CRM's, giving a team more time to load real pipeline data before deciding.

faq.q: Does either CRM charge a setup fee?
faq.a: No, neither Alpha CRM nor Beta CRM charges a setup fee on any published plan.

closing: Alpha CRM wins on trial length, free-plan headroom, and integration count, while Beta CRM only pulls ahead for a team that specifically wants its automation add-on and nothing else Alpha CRM offers.
